passage: You asked for a time someone said sorry properly? Okay. My mum, Farida. Before my board exams she screamed at me in front of my cousins about my mock marks, said I'd never amount to anything. I stayed at a friend's place that night. The next evening she came to pick me up. In the car she didn't even turn the radio on. She just said, "Omkar, what I said yesterday was cruel and untrue. I was scared about your exams, but that's mine to handle, not an excuse. I'm sorry." No "but you also". Nothing. I didn't know what to say, so I said "okay". We got pani puri on the way home. Weird thing is, I trust her more now than before the fight.

qa.q: Where did Omkar stay the night of the fight?
qa.a: Omkar stayed at a friend's place that night.

qa.q: How did Omkar feel when Farida apologised in the car, and what shows it?
qa.a: Omkar was surprised and unsure, not knowing what to say and managing only "okay".

qa.q: What made Farida's apology work?
qa.a: She named exactly what she had said, called it cruel and untrue, and said sorry without blaming Omkar, so it was a real repair.

qa.q: What might it have cost Farida to say sorry without excuses?
qa.a: She had to admit her own fear and set aside her pride, which is probably hard for a parent.

grounding: A teenager describes a mother who shouted cruelly, then came back, named it and apologised without excuses, which deepened trust.

passage: I'm Dolma, from the flat below. In the spring Farhan's father went away for work for three months and barely called. Farhan, fifteen, stopped coming to our evening football. When his father came back, I heard shouting at first, Farhan yelling, "You didn't even ring on my birthday!" Then the next evening I saw them on the stairs. His father was sitting two steps below him, saying, "You're right. I wasn't there, and I didn't call. That's on me, not the job. I'm sorry." Farhan didn't say anything. But on Sunday he was back at football, and his father stood at the edge of the field, watching the whole match.

qa.q: What did Farhan shout at his father?
qa.a: He yelled, "You didn't even ring on my birthday!"

qa.q: What might Farhan have been feeling when he stopped coming to football?
qa.a: He may have felt hurt and let down by his father's absence, and pulled away from things.

qa.q: What did the father's apology include that made it a real repair?
qa.a: He named what had happened, took the blame himself rather than blaming the job, and said sorry.

qa.q: How might Farhan's father feel watching the whole match on Sunday?
qa.a: He may feel relieved and grateful that Farhan is back, and keen to show he is present now.

grounding: A neighbour sees an absent father return, name his failure and apologise without excuses, and his teenage son slowly re-engage.

passage:
Tuesday: Vikas came home from a double shift and tripped over Nazia's school bag by the door. He shouted, loud enough for the neighbours, that she was careless and useless. Nazia went to her room and locked it.
Wednesday morning: He knocked before she left for school. "Last night I yelled at you and called you useless. That was wrong. I was tired, but that's not your fault, and it's not an excuse. I'm sorry." Nazia shrugged and walked out.
Saturday: Nazia sat on the arm of his chair while he watched cricket and said, casually, "You know, you're the only grown-up who says sorry like that." Then she told him about a fight with her friend.

qa.q: What did Vikas trip over?
qa.a: Nazia's school bag by the door.

qa.q: How might Nazia have felt when Vikas apologised on Wednesday?
qa.a: She was probably still hurt and wary, which is why she shrugged, even if the apology mattered to her.

qa.q: Which part of Vikas's apology made it a real repair?
qa.a: He named exactly what he did and refused to use tiredness as an excuse.

qa.q: How does the Saturday talk show the effect of the repair on Nazia?
qa.a: She trusts him again enough to share a fight with her friend, showing the relationship survived his mistake.

grounding: Shows over several days a parent who shouted, then names it and apologises without excuses, and the teen's trust returning.

passage: Your Bidisha-phuppi was sixteen when I missed her school play. I had promised. Instead I stayed at the shop counting stock and told myself she wouldn't mind. She minded. She didn't speak to me for a week, and I, Rafiq, stubborn old fool, said she was being dramatic. Then one night I passed her room and saw the costume still on the chair. I knocked. I didn't say "but the shop" or "but I was busy". I said, "I broke a promise to you, and I pretended it didn't matter. It did. I'm sorry." She cried, and I cried. After that, she told me things. Mistakes don't end a family, beta. Hiding them does.

qa.q: What did Rafiq see on the chair in Bidisha's room?
qa.a: The costume.

qa.q: How was young Bidisha feeling during the week of silence?
qa.a: She was hurt and let down that Rafiq broke the promise and then called her dramatic.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Seeing the costume made Rafiq knock and apologise plainly, without mentioning the shop or being busy.

qa.q: How did the apology change things for Bidisha?
qa.a: She cried with Rafiq and afterwards began sharing things, trusting that the bond could survive the mistake.

grounding: Shows a parent who broke a promise returning to name it and apologise without excuses, teaching a teen that bonds survive mistakes.

passage: The day Damini came back from a year of hospital work in Mumbai, the monsoon flooded their lane in Kolhapur, and she and Tarun were stuck indoors with no power. For the first hour he played games on his phone and answered in grunts. She had missed his birthday call, his exam results and two parent meetings. By candlelight she sat down opposite him. "I wasn't there this year. I didn't call when I said I would, more than once. I'm not going to tell you it was all for the family. I'm sorry, Tarun." He kept his eyes on the screen. Then the battery died. He looked up. "You missed my results." "Tell me now?" she asked. The rain kept falling. He told her.

qa.q: What flooded their lane in Kolhapur?
qa.a: The monsoon.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling during the first hour?
qa.a: He was hurt and angry at her absence, hiding behind his phone and answering in grunts.

qa.q: Why was Damini's apology effective?
qa.a: She named what she missed, didn't hide behind excuses about the family, and then invited him to share instead of lecturing.

qa.q: What would change if Damini had said the work was all for Tarun's sake?
qa.a: Tarun would likely feel his hurt was dismissed, and the silence between them might have continued.

grounding: Illustrates a parent who was absent returning, naming what she missed and apologising without excuses.

passage:
On Saturday, Uday's football final ended in a draw, and his father's seat in the stands stayed empty. That night, when Uday asked why, Irfan snapped, "Some of us have real work!" and slammed the door of their Andheri flat.
Uday didn't come out for dinner.
On Sunday morning, Irfan knocked and sat on the edge of the bed. He didn't mention work or traffic.
"I promised to come and I didn't. Then I shouted at you for asking. Both were wrong. I'm sorry."
Uday kept looking at the ceiling. "You always say you'll come."
"You're right to be angry. I can't undo Saturday. Next Sunday's match, I've told my boss I'm off."
A long pause. Then Uday sat up. "The replay's on my phone. Want to see my header?"
Irfan leaned in. "Show me."

qa.q: Where did Irfan's seat stay empty?
qa.a: In the stands at Uday's football final.

qa.q: How was Uday feeling on Sunday morning, and what shows it?
qa.a: He was hurt and angry; he kept looking at the ceiling and said, "You always say you'll come."

qa.q: What made Irfan's apology a real repair?
qa.a: He named both mistakes, missing the match and shouting, apologised without excuses, accepted Uday's anger, and made a concrete change for next Sunday.

qa.q: What would change if Irfan had blamed work instead of apologising?
qa.a: Uday would likely stay shut in and learn that his hurt doesn't matter, instead of learning that the relationship can survive a mistake.

grounding: Shows a father who missed his son's match and shouted, then returns to name it and apologise without excuses, repairing the bond.
